speechtext: The only increases are statutory increases.
There is an extra clerk in the first division of subdivision B.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, we have created an extra clerkship for the purpose of promoting the accountant, Mr. Campeau, who is at present at the maximum of the lower division and who is getting $2,800. We purpose recommending him for subdivision A of the first division.
Why is that done?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Campeau is an official of the department, having served 35 years, and he is a competent man. This is putting him on an equality with the accountants in the other departments.
Is there work for him to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, the chief ac countant in the Inland Revenue Department is a very important official of the department.
Is the accountant's branch made up of the seven clerks in the first division subdivision A and the first division, subdivision B?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They are not necessarily all in the accountant's branch. Mr Campeau is now in the first division, of subdivision B, and we propose to promote him. That will make one vacancy. We are creating one more clerkship for the purpose of promoting two clerks from subdivision A of the second division to subdivision B of the first division.
Who are being promoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have not decided yet. We are creating the vacancies. We have considered that probably, two of the best clerks at the head of the subdivision 'A' of the second division will receive the promotion. We are doing the same with regard to the next division. The vacancies created by these promotions will be filled by promotions from the lower division. In the second subdivision 'B' there is no change. There are four increases in the third division, subdivision A. This is simply making provision for promotion from the classes below under the Civil Service Act. There is an increase of two over the total employees of the department last year-44 instead of 42. The work of the department has been increasing. Last year we passed the Commercial Feeding Stuffs Act which comes into force the 1st of January and the Patent Medicine Act, which entailed additional work, and" we are providing for two extra clerks if required. -They are not yet appointed.	[DOT]

The minister has not given much information or reasons. He sets out with the idea that it is his duty to deplete the lower division and get the men into the higher division as quickly as possible. He has taken half from the third division, subdivision B, and put them into a higher division. There is something to be said in favour of promoting men, but if the minister is going to bestow all his activity in putting people up from lower divisions to higher divisions, he will soon have no lower divisions at all. What salaries are these four in the third division, whom he proposes to put into subdivision A, now getting? and what work are they doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There are no promotions from third division, subdivision A.
What about third division, subdivision B?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said that I was striving to promote from one division to another. Well, there are no promotions from third division, subdivision A, but I propose to move some from subdivision B to subdivision A of the third subdivision.
What are the reasons you are promoting these four?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
These clerks are largely statistical and are doing very good work. They are now receiving the maximum of the salary in their class and are deserving of promotion. Several of them have been a long time in the service. It is proposed to promote them and give them the minimum salary of subdivision B, to be strictly in accord with the spirit and intention of the Act. They can only get

their promotions on the recommendation of the deputy minister and the approval of the commission.
Would the minister give me the names of the four who are to be promoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Their names are
Yetts, Lyon, Allen and Lewis. They are the senior clerks in that division.
How long has Mr. Yetts been in the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Since 1895. Mr. Lewis came in - on the reorganization of the service, but was employed temporarily before that for about two years. Mr. Allen
has been in the service about two years and Mrs. Lyon about two years.
Will the minister kindly give me the names of the four left in possession, and state how long they have been in the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Arthur Robert came into the service in 1901, Ekins in 1907, Tee-vens in 1907 and Cantin in 1908.

If you are going to recompense those who have been longest in the service, Mr. Yetts, who came in in 1905, has a fair claim to promotion. You have promoted one who has been only two years doing temporary work, while Robert, who has been eight years in the service, and is I suppose at the maximum of his staff, is left. What is it debars him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is all a question of the ability of the clerks. Those I have named are, in the opinion of the deputy minister, the ones most efficient and most worthy of promotion at the present time. The whole matter of promotion is absolutely in the hands of the deputy minister, subject of course to the Civil Service Commission.

I do not know the clerks myself, and cannot pass any opinion on them. In that respect I suppose I am pretty much in the same position as the minister. who says he leaves all the promotions to his deputy. I am inclined to think that he has sometimes ideas of his own on the subject. If he left it entirely with the deputy, I am inclined to think that the proper ones would be apt to get promoted.
Department of Inland Revenue-contingencies, $8,000.
I see that B. C. Nicholas has an account of $609.30 for travelling expenses. Who is B. C. Nicholas?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He is my private secretary.

Does not the minister think it would be more the square deal not to shoulder off on Mr. Nicholas the charge Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
of $609 for flaunting around the country when it is really the minister who has been doing it? The only justification for paying Mr. Nicholas $609 for travelling expenses is that he has been on some official business. Was he on some official business, or was he accompanying the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend will probably see in the Auditor General's Report a small charge for travelling expenses for the minister.
That is what I complain of. The minister is a larger man, and why does he not bear his own expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman does not accuse me of charging^ to my private secretary a sum of money which I have expended-because that is the suggestion. The travelling expenses of my private secretary w'ere incurred on a visit to Nova Scotia and on a visit to British Columbia, accompanying me in both cases. I assume that the difference in our expenses is due to the fact that, like my hon. friend, I travel on a pass while my private secretary does not.

Does the minister not travel in a special private car, in which his private secretary would travel also, at no expense to the country beyond the cost of hauling the car? I would be surprised to find the minister travelling in an ordinary car such as we common mortals on this side of the House travel in. In the west during the last summer I did not find any of the ministers travelling otherwise than in a special car.
You did not look very hard then.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) looks at me because I found him travelling as a pilgrim in the pilgrim car.
I was delighted to meet you too.	'

I was delighted to meet the minister because he treated me to a very nice dinner. I had a foretaste of what may happen some day when members on this side of the House will have an opportunity of going on pilgrimages. Surely the Minister of Inland Revenue is not going to travel in a less gentlemanly way than the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Militia or the Minister of Agriculture.
Did the Minister of Agriculture travel through the west in a private car?
I did not see him in one.
Or anywhere else

Possibly he does not. I think when he went to Halton to try to induce the farmers there to elect a doctor from Toronto to represent them, he travelled in a very plain way and tried to show himself as the friend of the farmer. I may be mistaken, possibly the Minister of Agriculture does not travel in a special car, but I would be surprised if a minister from British Columbia would come down here and go down to Nova Scotia and not travel in a special car. I thought that every one of the ministers had a private car. Perhaps the minister can explain whether he actually did travel in a private car and that may explain how it was that the expenses of his private secretary were so large as compared with his own.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If it is of any interest to the House I have no objection to stating the facts. I do not think the hon. gentleman will find very excessive travelling expenses against either my private secretary or myself. I was in Nova Scotia on one occasion on an official visit but I was not in a private car, I paid my Pullman car accommodation to the Intercolonial railway and my private secretary did the same. " I was in British Columbia a year or two ago in company with Mr. Brock, director of the Geological Survey, visiting all the mines. On that occasion I had the use of a government car, an old private car which was very useful, indeed, as we stopped at all the small places from the Crows-nest to the west end of the Columbia & Western and the Victoria & Eastern road. Without a private car it would have been absolutely impossible to have visited very many of the small mining towns of British Columbia. On my last visit to the west I travelled as my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) travelled and paid my Pullman fare as he did. I met him in Vancouver and I do not think he saw me in a private car. I do not think the ministers generally, travel in private cars to any extent, but I would certainly do so if I thought it necessary. It was sometimes necessary in my case, not only in order to be able to live in the car, but to_ receive visits from persons interested, for instance, in mining.

I would not have interjected anything if the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) had not said that he met ministers in the west who had been travelling in private cars. I happen to be one of the ministers who spent a good deal of time in the west this summer and I asked him if he met me in a private car. If I had felt it to be in the interest of the public to carry a private car with me I would have done so. As a matter of fact I find it more convenient not to have one, and generally do not have one. I do not think that on any trip around the country I have
taken a private car. I can understand that ministers may find it more convenient to do so and if they do find it more convenient I think they should take the .car.

Perhaps the Minister of Railways would explain how the expense of hauling private cars over other lines than government lines is met. Do the ordinary railways charge so much a mile for hauling a private car or do they haul it free of expense?

When a minister takes an official car he makes his own arrangement with tjie railways as to its transportation. The Minister of Railways on account of the position he holds, is entitled to free transportation on any railway in Canada and he gets free transportation for his car on any railway in the United States as well. My department is under compliment to the railways for hauling a car, in fact I have been censured several times modestly by managers of railways because I did not take my car, as they always took theirs. When any other minister takes a car he makes his own arrangements for its transportation.
What is that arrangement?
I do not know.
The Minister of Public Works travels sometimes in a private car. Perhaps he would inform the House how the expense of hauling the car is arranged with other railways than the Intercolonial railway.	.

In the accounts of my department it will not be found that any charge has been made for the transportation of my not private but official car. I never travel in a private car. The car is an official car where I transact the business of my department when I travel, but as far as possible I very much prefer to travel in an ordinary Pullman. It is very much more expensive to the Minister to get a car from the Department of Railways than to travel in an ordinary Pullman. I find that we have to pay for all our food and even to pay the laundry bills and in going a comparatively short distance as to St. John and other places in New Brunswick I have found it very much more expensive to engage a car from the Railway Department than to travel in the Pullman and pay my own expenses, and ordinarily I take the Pullman. During the last summer I made an official visit ito the Northwest. It became necessary for me to stop off at a great many different places where public works are either under construction or in contemplation. I found that I could not possibly attend to that work without having an official car, and I did arrange to have it. And the Canadian Pacific railway very

kindly transported the car free of charge over its railway-it extended me' that courtesy. The same was done by the Canadian Northern.

I do not think that anyone objects to the Minister of Public Works or any other minister, when on public business that requires it, using an official car. But I was a little surprised to find, from the statement of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), that in such cases the minister was called upon to meet the expenditures for food, laundry, etc., used in his private car. Have I understood it aright?
That is the case.

I was under the impression that I had seen in the Auditor General's Eeport on several occasions charges for supplies on private cars. I do not say that any of these was in connection with the private car of the Minister of Public Works, as I do not remember. But I am a little surprised, and I think other members of the House will be surprised, to find that the minister himself pays these expenditures for provisioning and other charges in connection with his official car out of his own pocket.

That not only includes all supplies of every kind for the minister himself, but for every person who is travelling with him, and also the attendants upon the car. So, all the expenditures of every kind in the way of supplies, laundry and so on are paid by the minister who is travelling.
And the minister makes no claim for that on the public treasury?

Unless he might do it in the way of travelling expenses. I do not say he does.
Department of Labour-Salaries, $32,300; Contingencies, $12,000.

I may mention that there is a clerical error in the explanation of this item of salaries. In the fourth line, relating to second division, subdivision 'A', it is stated that there are two clerks at $800. That should read one clerk at $800. Then, in the sixth line, referring to third division, subdivision B, instead of one clerk at $800, it should be two at $800. This is a mere reversal of the figures and does not add to the total.

It seems to me that, if it appears in the estimate as third division, subdivision B, one clerk at $800, the minister cannot make it two. I should be inclined to think that could only be done by a supplementary estimate.
It will not change the total amount asked for, but merely reverses the figures.
Are any of these employees now in the eastern provinces making an investigation of the coal strike?

The deputy minister of the department has made a full investigation into the situation there and has prepared a careful report on the whole situation, which report I shall be glad to lay on the table of the House in the course of a day or so.
How long is it since that report was completed?
It is some weeks since it was prepared.
And will it be placed on the table at an early day?
I think I can promise it for Monday possibly.
How many employees are there in the Labour Department at Ottawa?
At present nineteen.
I see that there are two extra in the second division, subdivision A. Will the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The details are given on page 26 of the estimates.
But what we want is the reason.

That is the item I called attention to. - There should be only one clerk at $800. That provides for an additional
clerk one with a knowledge of French.
But there is an addition of two besides.
One is a stenographer and the other is accountant.
At what salary does the stenographer enter?

At $500. The additional clerk to take the position of accountant is provided for in in the second division, subdivision A, a clerk at $1,200. Heretofore the accounting of the department has been carried on by the accountant of the Post Office Department. But now that the Department of Labour has been given a separate standing in the service, it is proposed to have an accountant of its own.
But there are two additions in the third division, subdivision B. One is a stenographer at $500 and what is the other?
A stenographer at $800, one with a knowledge of French to assist in the correspondence.
Why does he enter at the maximum of his class?

I think it would be impossible to find a clerk at less than $800 who would carry out the work satisfactorily. Something more than the ordinary routine work is required of the one in this position.
v. Mr. FOSTER. But the schedule provides that in this class they commence at $500 and go up to $800. If clerks are to be appointed at the maximum, you might as well have no Civil Service Act at all.
Would*the minister (Mr. King) be good enough to give us a general idea of what these officials in the department are doing?

It would take some little time to outline, even in a very general way, the work of the officials of the department. But I may say that the department publishes a monthly journal, the ' Labour Gazette '. Several officers conduct investigations and compile reports and statistical tables relating to strikes and lockouts, changes in the rates of wages the cost of living, industrial accidents, and like subjects. The services of others are made necessary by the Industrial Disputes' Act, establishing boards under that Act, carrying on correspondence and the preparation of the reports sent by the different parties concerned. There are also officers whose duty it is to prepare schedules of wages for insertion in public contracts-the fair wage officers. They travel in different parts of the Dominion and investigate what are fair rates of wages to be paid for the different classes of labour on wmrks being carried on for the government. Then there is a great deal of correspondence in the department itself, in the nature of answers to inquiries in regard to industrial questions in this country, wages changes, and a great variety of subjects. There is also a great deal of correspondence from other countries and from individuals, as to the working of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. Then there are other officials of the department who are engaged in the work of translating, as the 'Labour Gazette' is published in French as well as English. There are also clerks who have to keep track of the expenditures, and the amounts derived from the sale of the 'Labour Gazette', subscription lists and such work as newspaper offices are obliged to do. There is also a library in the department under the charge of a clerk.
Do contingencies include the cost of printing the ' Labour Gazette ' ?
No.
Does this item include payment of correspondents of the ' Labour Gazette ' all over the country?
No, that comes under the general estimates. The cost of printing and publishing the ' Labour Gazette ' includes the amounts paid to correspondents.
How many copies of the ' Labour Gazette ' are issued, and to whom are they issued?

The department ha.s a list of paid subscribers numbering, I think, about 9,000. Then there is a free_ list, including secretaries of the trade unions, boards of trade, members of both Houses of parliament, labour departments in other countries, and societies with which we exchange periodicals. Altogether about 14,000 copies of the ' Gazette ' are issued each month.
What is the revenue obtained from paying subscriptions?

The revenue as given in the Auditor General's Report last year is $1,669.82. The amount charged for the ' Labour Gazette ' is 20 cents per annum. Bound copies of the ' Labour Gazette ' are sold at 50 cents a copy. The revenue of the department is derived from the sale of bound copies, and from the sale of individual copies, and the general subscriptions.
Where is the " Labour Gazette ' printed?

The department obtains the ' Gazette ' from the King's Printer. There have 'been times when the Printing Bureau has been much crowded, and the King's Printer has found it neces-sarv to have his own arrangements. But as far as our department is concerned, we deal with the King's Printer.

I see that there is $600 here for ' Allowance for private secretary.' Why it is necessary to make that allowance? Why could not a clerk in the department do the work of a private secretary?

The other clerks of the department have their specific duties to perform and therefore they are not available for this work. The secretary is a very hard worked official. His time is not his own. Regular clerks work the prescribed hours only. He gives virtually his entire time to the duties he has to perform. My secretary, Mr. Francis W. Giddens has frequently worked with me four nights in a week from seven until twelve o'clock, and I would like to say of him that a more faithful or ef-| ficient officer in the discharge of his duties is not to be found in the public service.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that a great many Japanese who were American citizens came, over from this United States during the recent fishing season and obtained employment in the fisheries in British Columbia waters. I would like to ask the minister how it was that these Japanese, who were American citizens, came to be employed in Canada. It occurred to me that probably the Department of Labour, being alive to the interests of that class of labour and having seen this statement reported in the press, and had got busy and ascertained why these men had obtained this employment thus depriving a certain number of Canadian fishermen of the livelihood that they were entitled to. Perhaps the minister could tell me if he has any information on that subject?

In regard to that I would say that any department of government would hardly find it expedient to act on reports that appear in the press from time to time. This particular report of which the hon. gentleman has spoken did not come to my notice. Had the matter beef) as serious as it appears to have been, the parties, one would think, would have been sufficiently .interested to have notified the department of a case of that sort and requested an investigation. If a notification of that kind were to come to the department an investigation certainly would be proceeded with, if it fell within the scope of the department's work. It is quite possible that in the case which has been mentioned these men may have been employed in violation of some existing Act, in the event of which there would have been redress in the courts, but without the particulars having been presented to the department in a formal way I hardly think the department would have been justified in proceeding of its own accord.
I might ask the minister whether that would come within the scope of the duties of the local correspondents, whether they are supposed to take cognizance of a thing of that kind.

Correspondents are expected to report on matters in their districts of interest to the department, correspondents are not informants expected to notify the department of the violations of any existing laws; they are to send in records of the actual happenings in their district so as to furnish statistical and descriptive records.

There is a correspondent at Vancouver and another at Westminster and this matter was very conspicuous in the press there. It seems to me the Labour Department could not be more usefully employed than in taking up a matter of that kind which is not the busi-Mr. KING.
ness of any person in particular who is not in the government service. How are the correspondents of the ' Labour Gazette ' appointed? Are they recommended by the labour organizations or by the political organizations. '

The department has sought to secure as correspondent some person who is thought to be persona grata to the industrial classes, not necessarily the labour element alone, but employers as well. Before any appointment has been made the department has as a rule ascertained from different sources the standing of those to be appointed. In some instances recommendations has been made by the member, in which cases further communication may have been had with other parties to ascertain the standing of the person recommended. The appointments are not made as political appointments at all. I am not aware of any having been so made and I should be very sorry to see them made for that reason

Would the minister consider it the duty of the department, now that attention has been called to the matter, to find out how these Japanese who are American citizens, came to be working in Canada under the guise of British subjects and having licenses issuable only to British subjects. Will the minister investigate and endeavour to protect the labourers on the Fraser river?

I should like to look carefully into all the circumstances to see whether it properly comes within the jurisdiction of the department to do what the hon. gentleman suggests. If on investigation I find that to be so I will certainly he pleased to follow it up.
Is it a fact that the ' Labour Gazette ' is printed in an office outside of the Government Printing Bureau?

At present I understand that is the case. The pressure of work has been such that the King's Printer found it impossible to print the ' Labour Gazette ' at the Bureau, and he made an arrangement with an outside office to do the printing.	.
What office?

I understand that the Ottawa ' Free Press ' is where the ' Gazette ' is being, printed at the present time. The King's Printer has made an arrangement, I understand, having in view what lie regarded as the best arrangement to make.
I presume the King's Printer called for tenders?
I presume so, but it not being in my department I cannot say.

This ' Labour Gazette ' according to the imprint is printed by ' C. H. Parmelee, Printer to the Ring's Most Excellent Majesty ' and on it there is a union label. I find that on a copy of the estimates which I have in my hand there is no union label. Does that explain the different fashion of printing these two official documents?

Some nine or ten years ago when the ' Labour Gazette ' was first published the union label was put on as an indication that the work was being performed under fair conditions. I understand that the Government Printing Bureau was an open shop, but notwithstanding that, the conditions were such that those controlling the label authorized the Printing Bureau to use it on the ' Labour Gazette.' As it was a publication which was circulating largely among the working classes it was thought advisable to have the label put on it under these circumstances, and there does not seem to be any reason to discontinue the practice.

That is, that in the case of a publication circulating largely among the labouring classes the union label is attached in order to lead the labouring classes to believe that the government printing is carried on under the conditions called for by the' appearance of that union label, whereas as a matter of fact the government printing is not carried on under these conditions, and the government printing office is not what they call a fair office, to take tlie expression used by the minister.
I do not remember having used the expression ' fair ' office.
My hon. friend beside me tells me that the expression used by the minister was ' open shop.' I believe the open shop is not recognized by union labour as the ideal condition.

I think that many trade unionists would prefer to have the closed shop, but I do not think that trade unionists necessarily hold that because a shop is an open shop the conditions may not be as fair as they are in a closed shop. The conditions that are important to labour are the hours of labour, the wages paid, and the sanitary conditions under which the employees work; all of these conditions are excellent 'at the Government Printing Bureau. That being so those who are interested in seeing such conditions furthered by means of the label were quite agreeable that the label should be put on the ' Labour Gazette ' when it was printed at the Government Bureau notwithstanding that the Bureau was not a closed shop.
I understand the minister to say that the label was attached as an indication that the work was performed under fair conditions.
That is exactly what I said.
Does not the union label usually mean that the shop is not an open shop?
It usually does mean that, but not always.
This is one illustration. Are there any others?
I think there are others.
Could the minister name one?
I could not name one at the moment, but I have no doubt that with a little research I could find one.

Last session I asked the then Minister of Labour whether he would be kind enough to use his influence with the Postmaster General to have the fair wage clause inserted in all postal contracts. I suppose that, owing to the relationship then existing between the Minister of Labour and the Postmaster General, he handed that matter over to his successor. I would like to ask the present Minister of Labour whether he has discussed that with the Postmaster General, and whether there is any prospect of the fair wage clause being attached to contracts of the Post Office Department.

My present impression is that the fair wage clause forms a part of every contract of the Post Office Department. In connection with contracts for postal supplies, such as letter carriers' uniforms and the like, the Department of Labour has been asked to approve of schedules of rates of wages of firms tendering for this class of work before the Post Office Department would make the contract, and I believe that in some cases contracts have been refused by the Post Office Department because of the unwillingness of some firms to pay what were regarded as fair and reasonable wages.
Are we to understand that the Postmaster General submits all mail to the Minister of Labour and receives from him an opinion whether they provide for the payment of fair wages for the work performed?

I was speaking with reference to supplies furnished to the Post Office Department. I had not in mind the question of carrying the mails. I have no doubt, however, that the desire of the Postmaster General would be to see that a fair rate of wages was paid to everybody engaged in that work, and if it became apparent that such was not the case, I am sure that he would be willing and glad to confer with the Department of Labour on the subject.	,

I would ask the Minister of Labour to be good enough to take that up with the Postmaster General, because I know that in my part of the country the pay of the Post Office Department for services of that kind is most miserable, and does not at all approximate to what in our country is considered fair wages. I am sure that he could not do a more popular act than to secure the reform I have suggested from the Post Office Department.
Department of Labour - contingencies,
512,000.
Is there any increase in that?

There is an increase, which however is more apparent than real. Heretofore the amount of money required for purposes included under the head of contingencies has been voted in the miscellaneous vote, which covered the entire expenditure of the Department of Labour. This year the amount has been separated so as to bring the contingencies under one head. Against an increase of $10,550 there should be offset a reduction of $7,400 in the vote being asked this year as compared with 1909-10, whh'h makes a net increase of only $3,150. Such items as printing and stationery, sundries and clerical and other assistance, will hereafter be paid out of contingencies, in conformity with the practice in other departments. I might say that the staff is larger than before. The minister's office and the minister's secretary's office come into consideration in this connection, as well as expenses for travelling on the part of the fair wage officers and other officers connected with the administration of the Industrial Disputes Act and other measures There is also an additional amount put in to enable the department to purchase necessary books and periodicals.
Department of Customs-salaries, $244,975.
I suppose the minister thinks the increase is worthy of a little explanation.

But we are not asking for that much more money, because Mr. KING.
certain officers have replaced other officers at lower Tates of salary. Burns in the third division at $750, resulting in a decrease of $50. Then, a vacant clerkship in the second division B, at an estimated salary of S800, caused by the resignation of F. A. This vacancy is estimated to be filled by the appointment of a clerk in the same division at a minimum salary of $800. There is a decrease there of $350. Mr. Methot, a clerk in the second division, subdivision B, whose estimated salary for 1909-10, w^as $1,200, was replaced by Mr. A. B. Sowter, an officer of the outside service at Winchester, B.C., who came in at $1,000, a decrease of $200. A vacancy in the third division, subdivision A, caused by the resignation of J. N. Cram, whose estimated salary was $950, was filled by the appointment of Mr. A. S. Ogilvy at the minimum salary of $500, a decrease of $450. Allowing for these reductions, we have $3,675 as the net increase that we are providing for. The six additional officers we propose to bring in, and for whom we provide $4,800 are expected to be required, perhaps, in the statistical branch, owing to the operation of the French treaty. Of course, we must keep a detailed record of that trade for statistical purposes. Hitherto, under the more limited treaty that has been in existence, there was not much work involved, but the new treaty with its wider scope will make necessary additions to the staff of the Statistical Department.
I do not understand that. Why should it be so?

We shall have to open another set of books and have a special column in our returns because of the treaty. With the few articles coming in under the old treaty, the clerks'could note these entries as they came to them and make up their tables with comparatively little labour. But now this special column will have to be added, and we shall be able to give, month by month, in our unrevised statement, statistics with reference to that trade.

I would like to understand the minister's theory on this subject. What is it that makes the preparation of these statistics, more difficult? Suppose there were no treaty at all, and you had exactly the same amount of imports and exports, would these additional assistants be required? I ask purely for information.

I do not wonder that the hon. member (Mr. R. L. Borden) asks the question for I asked it myself when the proposition first came before me The same idea occurred to me that, I suppose, is in the mind of the hon. member-that if more goods come in from France there might be so many less come in from other countries. But, under the old treaty, when an invoice came before our statistical officers, they could pick out the articles coming under the treaty, as they were few, and by merely keening a running memorandum, it was easy to sum them up. But now that the French treaty will embrace a very large number of articles, and with other nations as well as France receiving the benefit of this most favoured nations treatment, there will be many shipments coming in under the treaty-most of them from France, of course, but some from other countries, making it necessary to keep, day by day, a regular tabulated record which will show the workings of the treaty.

I do not know whether I understand it yet. Is" it because the officers are obliged to apply a third tariff, the intermediate tariff, or is it because the government anticipate a larger importation, or both?
It is the intermediate tariff.
That is, you have a third tariff?
Yes, I should have said that.
The minister thinks it really necessary to have these additional officers?

I questioned it, just as the hon. member does. It was explained
to me. But I further put my officers under promise that unless they found these additional officers to be necessary, they are not to be put on. My officers promised that unless these men are required they will not be put on. Of course these work with other clerks, certain officers take the port of Montreal, others the port of Toronto, and the work will be divided in that way. It may be that we will not have to put on six men.
There is a very simple alternative, to repeal the intermediate tariff.
Oh, yes, but what a misfortune that would be.
To these men who would not get their appointments. As far as the country is concerned, it would be far quicker.

Is it proposed to have a separate column for every country that will enjoy the same privileges as France enjoys or will all countries that come under that intermediate tariff be thrown together? If so I do not see that it will afford us much information as to the extent to which our trade with France will be improved under this French treaty.

The intention is to have on the margin the countries for which goods are imported as they are in the general tariff in the trade and navigation returns now. We will apply the same thing to the intermediate tariff so that you will see what other countries are participating and to what extent the trade with France has developed.
Then we will have to go all through the trade and navigation returns to see what that increase is.
Unless we do it for you. We have summaries and we will try and do that.
What is the meaning of the increase in contingencies?

Under the Civil Service Act we are empowered to employ clerical and other assistance temporarily as for instance in the case of the illness of an official but without such a vote as this there is no provision for paying these extra clerks. I cannot say that all or any of this will be expended.

The commissioner
recommends it, does he?

Oh surely.
Department of Railways and Canals-Civil government, salaries including M. J. Butler at .$8,000, $130,187.50.

GRAHAM (Minister of
Railways and Canals). By a glance at the

estimates, it will be seen there is a reduction of $9,500. The number of clerks is reduced by six. In one division there is an increase of one. That is caused by the promotion of Mr. Little, the accountant in the department, to the first division subdivision A, which was done in the usual way through the Civil Service Commission. During the last five years I think Mr. Little has handled oyer $139,000,000. He is one of the most important officials we have and has been in the service some 28 years. That is the only increase in any class and there is a decrease in the total expenditure of $9,500.
It is interesting to observe that a decrease is really an increase. Where is the increase in this case?

There is absolutely no increase in the total. The decrease comes from the fact that while some officials have statutory increases, and Mr. Little's salary will be increased in promoting him from one class to the other, we drop some six clerks from the total that weTe in the estimates of last year. So we have a net increase in the expenditure of $9,500.
Is there an actual decrease in the number of clerks employed?

The decrease is rather in the estimate of last year. We had several vacancies in the department, and in our reorganization I came to the conclusion that we could get along without filling those vacancies, and they are dropped from the reorganization.
Contingencies, $15,000.
This is the same figure as it has been for years.
What is the item of $10,000 expended for printing and stationery?

There is all the printing and stationery for the department, for instance, the annual report. There is almost an unlimited quantity of stationery used in the various branches of the department, books and stationery of all kinds. Besides the annual report, special reports have to be printed.
Does $10,000 cover all that?
It covers the departmental printing.
I must compliment the minister on his economy. I should expect it more likely to be $30,000.
That does not cover the printing for the railway?
Not for the Intercolonial, the Intercolonial pays for its own report.
Is it the intention to start a purchasing agency in Ottawa to buy supplies for the Intercolonial?

Yes, in connection with the Intercolonial we are establishing a purchasing agency. Of course that will come in the Intercolonial estimates. But we intend to have a purchasing agency under the direct control of the department.
Where is this printing done?
I think our departmental work and our reports are all printed at the Printing Bureau, but I am not positive. It all comes through the King's Printer at least.

So did the report of-the Department of Labour come through the King's Printer, it bore his impress, and yet it seemed to have been farmed out. I do not know whether the Minister of Railways is engaged in farming operations as well as the Minister of Labour.
The head of the Printing Bureau would have to say that, personally I do not know. We get our report from the King's Printer, I imagine it is done at the Printing Bureau.
Are tenders asked for the supply of any of this stationery?
I stated before that we do not ask for tenders for stationery, our printed material is supplied by the King's Printer. The head of that department would be able to say how it is done.
I understand your printing is done there, I was referring to stationery.
There is a stationery department to which all requisitions go for stationery.
Who is the head of that department?
The Secretary of State is the head of the Printing Bureau, and of the Stationery Department as well.
When the Secretary of State is here he will be able to show that it is all right.

He may be able to say it is all right, but he ought to be here to say it. It is not satisfactory to be told that we should get information from some one else who is not here. If that information is necessary from some one else, that person ought to be here to give it.
Does the hon. gentleman mean the supplying of stationery to all the departments?

An inquiry is made as to whether there are tenders; the

minister says he does not know, we will have to apply to the head of some other department. Then I say if we are to apply to the head of some other department that head ought to be here to give the information.
He will no doubt give it when he is here passing the estimates in his department.

So far as an item in any department is concerned, we do not ask for tenders, we send a requisition for it. When the Department of the Secretary of ' State comes up, all this will be a matter for criticism, how he does all this.
In the meantime you have got your money voted.
This is the first time I have learned that you apply to the Secretary of State with your requisitions for stationery. All I have heard mentioned before was the Printing Bureau.

My hon. friend will understand that no person has said that he applied to the Secretary of State. Requisitions are made to the King's Printer. The question was asked who is the head of the department; it is the Secretary of State.
Certainly he is the King's Printer for the purpose of giving information to this House. Is it a charge from one department to the other, as if it were an actual purchase, or what is the system?
I think you will find we are responsible to the King's Printer in cash, as if it were a transaction betwen our department and some outside printing establishment.
He supplies the other departments at certain prices, and the question is whether or not, in laying in those supplies, he adopts the system of tender, and no one knows anything about it.
He will be able to tell you that.
I have no doubt he does apply for tenders in many cases.

We tried to obtain from the Minister of Labour some information in regard to the printing done in the Printing Bureau, and he finally gave us to understand that it was done by the Free Press Printing Company in this town, and apparently not done by tender at all. That item this year amounts to $23,300. Certainly it is a proper question to ask, and there should be some information.
Perhaps the head of that department will say when his department is under discussion that he did get tenders for it.
All we could get from the Minister of Labour was that the Printing Bureau did the work, and that he knew nothing further about it.

As to buying by tender, knowing something about buying paper and supplies of that kind, I am inclined to think that when the Secretary of State comes to make his reply he will have to say that he buys his paper as any dealer does, getting it from the best people at the best price he can. Any man who is engaged in the paper business often buys his stock by tender.

The Minister of Customs says that this is a very proper question when the Secretary of State is in his place. What kind of a question is it when the secretary is not in his place? I remember an incident occurring once in a court in Nova Scotia where witness was trying to explain to counsel what kind of a dog a retriever was and finally, to make himself understood, he said: He is a dog which, if you throw your handkerchief away, will go and bring it to you, whereupon counsel responded: What kind of a dog is h& when you do not have any handkerchief?
Department of Marine and Fisheries-Salaries, $250,150.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: The amount voted last year for this item was $247,830. This year $250,150 is asked, or an increase of $2,320. The increase is made up as follows: In the first division, subdivision 'A', there i3 an increase of $600 to six officers who have not reached the maximum of their class. In the first division, subdivision 'B', there is a decrease of $750. The decrease is due to the fact that five of the officers who have reached the maximum salary have dropped out and their places will be filled by officers at the minimum salary.
What becomes of the officers who drop out? Do they go into some other branch?

Yes, they have gone up to some other branch or have left the service. There is the wreck commissioner, one hydrographer, one chief clerk, and the commissioner of lights. In the second division subdivision ' A,' there is an increase of $2,600 which is made up as follows: One translator at $1,600 and the statutory increase of $50 to each of the officers of this class who have not reached the maximum. Three who have reached the maximum salary have dropped out and their places are to be filled by officers at the minimum salary. In the second division, subdivision 'B', there is a decrease of $1,300. In the third division, subdivision 'A', there is an increase of $700 made up

of the statutory increases of $70 to each of the officers who have not reached the maximum of their class. In the third division, subdivision 'B', there are extra siiort-hand writers at the minimum salary of this class and there is also the statutory increase of $50 to each in this class. Deducting the decreases of $2,050 there is left an increase of $2,320.
Is this new naval vote going to be administered by the Department of Marine and Fisheries?
Yes.
Will there be any increase in the staff of the department for the administration of a service which is to cost nearly $3,000,000?

Most of the officers for the administration of this naval vote will be technical officers whom the British Admiralty are kind enough to loan us for the organization of the service, and as they cannot be under the regular Civil Service Act they will have to be paid out of the vote itself.
That is out of the $3,000,000?

Yes, out of the $3,000,-
000.
Do I understand the minister to say that these salaries are inclusive of the salary of the wreck commissioner?
Yes.
The wreck commissioner, I presume, is the officer who has charge of the inquiries into wrecks?
Yes.
When he does not attend himself he appoints some one else?

No, not himself. The minister has the right under the law to appoint any officer of the department, or any judge, for the purpose of making these inquiries. It need not necessarily be the wreck commissioner, but generally speaking we have a man who looks after this business and who is called the wreck commissioner. When the wreck commissioner is too busy, when he is doing something else or making some other inquiries, some one else may be appointed under the law by the minister for the purpose of making an inquiry.

Then it would be the minister who would issue the instructions to be followed by the commissioner who makes the investigation into the wreck? They would not come from the wreck commissioner but from the head of the department?

There are no special instructions given. There is simply an appointment made for the purpose of making the inquiry and the inquiry is then made under the provisions of the law.
Department of Marine and Fisheries-Contingencies, $30,000.

There is an increase of $7,000 made up as follows:	The amount
set apart for printing and stationery and other such services of the department for this current year was in excess of the amount which was voted and the expendi- .. ture would be so close as to require the cutting down of requisitions, such as for typewriters; so that we have to provide for a larger amount.
Where is this printing done?
It is done at the Printing Bureau. We send our requisitions for stationery and printing to the King's Printer, the accounts are sent to us and we have to pay them.

As the hon. the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) is in his place he could possibly tell us about the contracts which aTe let outside of the Printing Bureau. We have been asking for a good deal of information with regard to a number of contracts for printing and stationery which are let by tender or in what manner they were let.

I will be pleased to give my hon. friend all the information on this subject when the estimates for the Printing Bureau are up, but my present recollection of what has been done-is that there are few, if any, contracts outside of the Printing Bureau for printing.
We were able to find just a few minutes ago where one contract was let to the Free Press of Ottawa for some $20,000 odd. Perhaps the minister can tell us whether this was let by tender or not?
Was that last year or this?
There was over $30,000 worth of printing done for the Department of Labour last year.
I have not the information at hand, but I will be pleased to give my hon. friend all the information when the estimates for printing are under consideration.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has taken the position that the other ministers have taken this evening with regard to printing. He simply says that it is done at the Printing Bureau as far as he knows. He does not

know whether it is let by tender outside of that or not. We have been anxious to find whether the printing has been done outside of the Printing Bureau.
I will be pleased to give my hon. friend all the information on that point.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State if the printing is charged to each of the different departments at actual cost?
That is the procedure, as I understand.
Would the minister give us some idea what the $10,000 is needed for in the way of sundries?
Telephones, telegrams, newspapers and travelling expenses.
Travelling expenses if included as sundries would not appear as ' travelling expenses * in the Auditor General's Report.
This is a vote for contingencies and they are taken out of that.

A contingency is something that is unexpected, but travelling expenses are a thing that have to be paid every year. It would look as if the word ' contingencies ' was used to cover up something. I am not saying there is anything wrong about it, but the word is misleading and does not give us an accurate idea of what the money is intended for. The minister will remember that during the past year or two a good many suspicions have been aroused, and a thing of this kind is calculated to arouse suspicion. It is in the interest of the minister I make the suggestion.
The remarks of mv hon. friend will apply to all the departments because the word ' contingencies ' is used all through the estimates.
I quite understand that but it does not improve the situation.
How much of this vote was for travelling expenses last year?

The accountant has not the information, but I will procure it later.
Department of Justice-Salaries (including E. L. Newcombe, $7,000), $103,498.75.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An additional stenographer is provided for this year to commence with a salary of $500.
Who decides that an extra clerk is necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It lias been discussed with me by the deputy several times during the year as a matter of necessity. It
is within my own knowledge that this official is required, but it is entirely on his representation that I am proceeding.
I understand that the deputy minister recommends the appointment of a new officer. Who selects the officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The officer will be selected, of course, under the Civil Service Act by our applying for him to the Commission, and asking them to give us the name of some person competent to take this position. We have no idea who it will be.
Who makes the recommendation to the Civil Service Commission as to whom it should be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no recommendation to the Civil Service Commission. They have their list of candidates who have passed the examination, and under the statute they will simply make the appointment and send the person selected to the department to enter upon the duties of the office.
Will it be a person who has passed the Civil Service examination or one who intends to apply for examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It must, under the statute, be some person who has already passed.
It does not follow, then, that the person who receives the most marks will get the first appointment?
I think it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That depends upon the manner in which the statute is administered by the Commission, and my own idea was that it would be the person who obtained the highest number of marks, if that person were willing to take that position in preference to waiting for the next one that came.

I noticed lately that the deputy minister of justice has been practising in private cases before the Supreme Court. Not long ago he appeared as counsel for the province of Nova Scotia in a case in which the province of New'Brunswick was also a party. I have heard considerable criticism as to that. I must say that it does seem to me that a gentleman occupying the position of deputy minister of justice should not practise before the Supreme Court of Canada as counsel for private parties. I do not wish to make any reflection at all on the deputy minister of justice, because he is recognized by the profession throughout the country as a very able lawyer and a very efficient minister of justice; but it did seem to me that a gentleman occupying his position should

not practise before the court as counsel for private litigants.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The subject which the hon. gentleman has mentioned is one that I am probably in no better position to say anything upon than any other member of the House. I have never considered that it was my duty or my right to investigate what may be said to be the private affairs of the gentleman who happened to be the deputy minister of the Department of Justice. I think I am in a position to certify, as matter within my own knowledge, which I have learned within the last three years if I never knew it before, that it would be very difficult to find any man able to discharge the duties of the position which Mr. Newcombe occupies, as efficiently as he discharges them; and I think I am in a position to say also that he has never in any way neglected the duties of the office which he holds, or allowed any other considerations, such as those of business or even of recreation, to interfere with the efficient and faithful doing of his work as deputy minister. To what extent he may be given by professional friends who have confidence in him, briefs in the Supreme Court, I am not able to state; I have never made examination.
I know, just as my hon. friend knows, that occasionally there is an instance of that happening; it is not very frequent. I am able to say, however, that the doing of any such work, which is outside the regular work of the department, has never been allowed by Mr. Newcombe to interfere in the least degree with full attention to the duties of his position.

I hope the Minister of Justice did not understand me as suggesting that the appearance of Mr. Newcombe before the Supreme Court rendered him any less efficient as deputy Minister of Justice. My remarks were directed entirely to the question of his practising before the courts of the country as counsel for private litigants, in view of the relation he occupies towards those courts. The salary of the deputy Minister of Justice is $7,000, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, that is the statutory salary. As to the other items, I may say that there is no change whatever in the staff of the Supreme Court, except the statutory increases. In the Court of Exchequer an additional clerk is asked for. That clerk, the registrar says, the business of the court requires. He is to do the work of a stenographer, as the present staff of the court is not able to cope with that work without the aid from time to time of stenographers who are employed for temporary purposes. The salary of the new clerk, which it is proposed should be $2,100, is the lowest that an efficient man can be obtained for, and it-will be, perhaps not in whole Mr. CROCKET.
but in large part, met by the charges for copies of evidence, which are paid for by litigants before the court. .
